sentences.text: The next year, Tamar was twelve.
She came back to the ringing station in October.
She had thought about the reed warbler all year, off and on.

Sometimes at school she would suddenly think of her — probably eating an insect in a tree in central Africa right now — and she would smile a little, and her teacher would ask what she was thinking about, and she would say, nothing.
But she was thinking about a small bird whose ring number she had memorized.
She spent the first two weeks of that autumn helping her father, and every net check she made, she looked at each bird's legs before she looked at anything else.
Every day she hoped.
On the seventeenth day, she caught her.
She recognized the ring number before she even fully read it.
She knew the shape of the numbers.
She had drawn them in the margins of her school notebooks a hundred times.
It was the same bird.
She said, "Aba.
Aba.
She came back." Her father came over.
He looked.
He put his hand on Tamar's shoulder.
He said, softly, "So she did.
Fifth autumn.
That is very old for a reed warbler now.
She has beaten the odds."
In the lab that morning, they measured her again.
She was thinner than last year.
She had lost a little weight.
Her feathers were more worn.
She was starting to be an old bird.
Her father was quiet as he weighed her.
Then he said, "This might be her last one, Tamar.
I don't want to make you sad.
But you should know.
If we don't catch her again next year, it does not necessarily mean she died.
But it probably does." Tamar nodded.
She had thought about this.
She was ready to hear it, though hearing it still hurt a little.
When she released the reed warbler that day, she held her for a moment longer than she had needed to.
She looked at her.
She said, in a whisper only the bird could hear, "I don't know if I will see you next autumn.
But I hope so.
And if not, I hope you had a good year.
I hope you built a good nest.
I hope you had chicks.
I hope you got warm sometimes.
Have a safe flight south." And she opened her hand, and the bird flew, and Tamar watched her go, small and brown and heading south, and she waved.
She waved.
She could not help it.
Her father was watching.
He did not say anything about the waving.
But that evening, when they were making supper together, he said, "Tamar.
I want to tell you something.
What you did today — waving at her, saying goodbye — that is not scientific.
That is not what we are supposed to do.
But I did it too, in my head.
I said goodbye to her too.
Sometimes we do that.
The birds do not know.
But we know.
I want you to keep doing it.
Even when you are grown up and you are a scientist yourself.
Do not stop doing it.
It is important." Tamar nodded.
She said, quietly, "I won't stop."
The autumn Tamar was thirteen, the reed warbler did not come.
Tamar checked every net every day for three weeks.
She caught other birds.
She caught two reed warblers from other nesting populations, both freshly ringed by her.
But A-471-338 did not come.
Her father was gentle about it.
He did not press.
Tamar was quiet on the last day, when they packed up.
In the jeep going home she looked out the window at the desert and she thought about her bird.
Six autumns of life.
Six migrations.
Fifty thousand kilometers of flying.
And then, somewhere, this year, she had stopped.
Tamar said, "Aba.
Do you think she made it.
Or do you think she died on the way." Her father thought carefully.
He said, "I do not know.
Nobody knows.
That is the honest answer.
She had a good long life for her kind.
She probably raised many chicks.
She flew here and back many times.
She saw things we cannot even imagine.
What happened to her at the end — I don't know.
But she had a real life." Tamar nodded.
She kept looking out the window.
When she got home that autumn, Tamar started a small notebook.
On the first page she taped a tiny brown feather — one her father had let her keep, years before, from a bird that had died naturally in the mist net one hot afternoon.
Beside the feather, she wrote in her most careful handwriting: A-471-338.
European reed warbler.
Female.
Ringed 2023 in the Negev.
Not seen 2028.
Approximate distance flown in life: 50,000 kilometers.
Approximate weight: 11 grams.
Underneath, she wrote: I noticed her.
She was here.
I want to be someone who keeps noticing.
She looked at the page for a long moment.
She closed the notebook.
She would open it many times over the years.
She would fill it with other birds.
She would keep the record.
That was what she had learned in the Negev.
That the world was full of small persistent things that would go by unnoticed unless someone chose to notice them.
And she was choosing.
